title: How to Start a Hospice Program in Colorado

html:
Introduction

Hospice programs in Colorado represent a vital component of the state’s healthcare continuum, providing end-of-life care across home, residential, and facility settings. Operating under the regulatory oversight of the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE), Colorado’s hospice market offers moderate opportunity for new providers committed to compassionate care.

With approximately 82 licensed hospice providers statewide, capacity varies significantly by region. Urban centers such as Denver and Colorado Springs have higher provider density, while rural areas face moderate undersupply, creating pockets where demand exceeds available services. For entrepreneurs willing to navigate detailed regulatory compliance, hospice care offers both meaningful work and sustainable business opportunity.

This comprehensive guide walks you through every step of launching your hospice program in Colorado, from understanding regulations to building the interdisciplinary team that delivers exceptional end-of-life care.

Table of Contents

  • Understand Colorado’s Regulations
  • Choose the Type and Size of Program
  • Business Structure and Licensing
  • Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan
  • Secure a Suitable Facility and Location
  • Hire and Train Qualified Staff
  • Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans
  • Marketing and Community Outreach
  • Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Inspections
  • Frequently Asked Questions

1. Understand Colorado’s Regulations

Before launching your hospice program, you must thoroughly understand the regulatory framework governing hospice services in Colorado

Regulatory Framework

The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE) licenses hospice agencies in Colorado. Programs must comply with the Colorado Code of Regulations (CCR 10-CCR-2505-10-8.550) which governs hospice operations and benefit provisions.

State and Federal Requirements

Hospice providers must navigate dual regulatory systems:

State Licensure – CDPHE establishes Colorado-specific requirements for hospice operations, staffing, and services. State licensing is required before providing any hospice services.

Medicare Certification – Most hospice providers also seek Medicare certification, which requires compliance with federal Conditions of Participation (42 CFR Part 418). Medicare certification enables billing the Medicare Hospice Benefit, which covers the majority of hospice services nationally.

Medicaid Enrollment – Colorado Medicaid covers hospice services, requiring separate provider enrollment with the Department of Health Care Policy and Financing (HCPF).

Accreditation

While not required, many hospice programs seek voluntary accreditation from organizations such as:

  • The Joint Commission
  • Community Health Accreditation Partner (CHAP)
  • Accreditation Commission for Health Care (ACHC)

Accreditation demonstrates commitment to quality and may facilitate certain contracts.

2. Choose the Type and Size of Program

Selecting the right program model influences startup costs, staffing needs, and market positioning.

Hospice Care Settings

Home-Based Hospice is the most common model, providing services in patients’ residences. This model requires lower facility investment but robust field staffing and care coordination.

Inpatient Hospice provides care in dedicated facilities for patients requiring intensive symptom management or respite care. Capital requirements are significantly higher but may fill service gaps in underserved areas.

Facility-Based Contracts allow hospice providers to serve patients in nursing homes, assisted living facilities, and hospitals through agreements with those facilities.

Specialty Programs

High-demand niches include:

Pediatric Hospice Care – Specialized services for children with terminal illnesses address significant unmet need and require specially trained staff and family support services.

Culturally Specific Care – Programs tailored to Colorado’s diverse populations including Hispanic/Latino, Native American, and immigrant communities.

Rural Hospice Delivery – Models designed for efficient rural service delivery, potentially integrating telehealth capabilities.

Hospice-at-Home with Telehealth – Enhanced home care models utilizing telehealth for monitoring and family support.

Scale Considerations

New hospice programs often start serving 20-50 patients simultaneously, scaling as reputation and referrals grow. Smaller programs can maintain quality and personalized care while larger programs achieve economies of scale in administration and on-call coverage.

3. Business Structure and Licensing

Proper business and licensing foundations are essential for sustainable operations.

Entity Formation

Hospice programs may operate as:

For-Profit Entities – LLCs, corporations, or partnerships pursuing commercial hospice operations.

Nonprofit Organizations – 501(c)(3) entities, which may access certain grants and community support.

Hospital or Health System Affiliates – Programs operating under larger healthcare organization umbrellas.

Regardless of structure, obtain appropriate state registrations, tax identifications, and comprehensive insurance coverage.

CDPHE Licensing Process

Securing and maintaining licensure through CDPHE involves:

  • Pre-Application Planning – Review regulations, assess requirements, prepare documentation
  • Application Submission – Complete application with required attachments including policies, organizational charts, and service descriptions
  • Background Checks – Owners and key personnel undergo background screening
  • Facility Inspection – If operating inpatient facilities, physical inspection is required
  • Program Review – Policies, procedures, and clinical protocols reviewed for compliance
  • License Issuance – Upon approval, state license is issued

Medicare Certification

After state licensure, most programs pursue Medicare certification:

  • CMS Form 855A – Complete Medicare enrollment application
  • State Survey – CDPHE conducts survey on behalf of CMS to verify compliance with Conditions of Participation
  • Provider Number Assignment – Upon successful survey, CMS assigns Medicare provider number
  • Billing Activation – Establish electronic billing capabilities

The certification process typically takes 3-6 months after state licensure.

4. Develop a Comprehensive Business Plan

A solid business plan guides decisions and attracts necessary financing.

Market Analysis

Colorado has approximately 82 licensed hospice providers statewide. Urban regions have higher density while rural areas experience limited access. Research your target service area to identify:

  • Existing providers and their market positions
  • Underserved populations or geographic areas
  • Referral source concentrations
  • Community demographics and projected needs

While comprehensive statewide hospice-specific waiting list numbers are not publicly available, related HCBS waitlists exceed 700,000 individuals statewide, indicating substantial demand pressures.

Financial Projections

Startup Costs for hospice programs typically range from $250,000 to $500,000 for home-based programs, significantly more for inpatient facilities:

  • Licensing and certification: $25,000-$50,000
  • Initial staffing and training: $100,000-$200,000
  • Office space and equipment: $30,000-$75,000
  • Vehicles and medical equipment: $40,000-$100,000
  • Operating reserves: $100,000-$200,000

Revenue Model – Hospice reimbursement in Colorado aligns closely with Medicare rates. Routine home care per diem rates range approximately from $190 to $240 depending on level of care and setting. Medicaid pays roughly 95% of Medicare skilled nursing facility daily rates for hospice room and board services.

Hospice agencies operating at about 70-85% capacity report gross margins commonly ranging between 12%-18%, contingent on operational efficiency, payer mix, and length of stay. New hospice providers can expect a break-even timeline of approximately 9 to 12 months.

Payer Mix

Develop projections for:

  • Medicare Hospice Benefit (typically 80%+ of census)
  • Medicaid
  • Commercial insurance
  • Charity care/unfunded

5. Secure a Suitable Facility and Location

Facility needs depend on your service model.

Home-Based Hospice

For primarily home-based services, you need:

Administrative Office – Space for management, clinical coordination, and interdisciplinary team meetings.

Medical Supply Storage – Secure, climate-controlled storage for medications and medical equipment.

On-Call Coordination – Systems for 24/7 patient and family access to clinical staff.

Vehicle Fleet – Reliable transportation for field staff, or reimbursement systems for personal vehicles.

Inpatient Hospice Facility

If operating inpatient services, extensive facility requirements apply:

  • Patient rooms meeting privacy and comfort standards
  • Common areas for families and patients
  • Medication rooms and clinical areas
  • Kitchen and food service capabilities
  • Administrative and meeting space

Location Considerations

Geographic Coverage – Position centrally to your service area to minimize travel time for field staff.

Referral Proximity – Consider location relative to major hospitals, cancer centers, and physician practices.

Staff Recruitment – Choose locations accessible to the healthcare workforce you need.

6. Hire and Train Qualified Staff

The interdisciplinary team is the heart of hospice care.

Required Positions

Medical Director – Physician (MD or DO) providing medical oversight, participating in care planning, and certifying terminal prognosis. May be employed or contracted.

Hospice Administrator – Overall program management, regulatory compliance, and business operations.

Registered Nurses – Clinical assessment, care coordination, and skilled nursing services. Nurses often serve as case managers for assigned patients.

Licensed Practical Nurses – Support RNs with skilled nursing tasks under supervision.

Certified Nursing Assistants/Home Health Aides – Personal care, light housekeeping, and patient support under nursing supervision.

Social Workers – Psychosocial assessment, counseling, resource coordination, and family support. Master’s-prepared social workers required for certain functions.

Chaplains – Spiritual care and support for patients and families of all faith backgrounds.

Bereavement Coordinators – Grief support services for families for at least 13 months following death.

Volunteers – Trained volunteers provide companionship, respite, and other non-clinical support. Regulations require volunteer programs.

Staffing Challenges

Reports from hospice providers reference delays caused by nursing shortages and resource constraints. Develop competitive compensation packages and supportive work environments to attract and retain qualified staff.

Training Requirements

All clinical staff must maintain current licensure/certification. Additional training includes:

  • Hospice philosophy and interdisciplinary care
  • Pain and symptom management
  • Psychosocial and spiritual care
  • Communication skills for end-of-life conversations
  • Regulatory compliance and documentation
  • Cultural competency

7. Policies, Procedures, and Care Plans

Comprehensive policies demonstrate compliance and ensure consistent, quality care.

Required Policies

Hospice programs must maintain policies addressing:

  • Admission and Eligibility – Terminal prognosis criteria, election statements, consent procedures
  • Clinical Care – Pain management, symptom control, medication management
  • Interdisciplinary Team – Composition, meetings, care planning processes
  • Patient Rights – Advance directives, informed consent, complaint procedures
  • Volunteer Program – Recruitment, training, supervision, documentation
  • Bereavement Services – Assessment, service delivery, duration requirements
  • Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement – Data collection, analysis, improvement projects
  • Emergency Preparedness – Disaster planning, patient evacuation, continuity of care
  • Infection Control – Prevention, surveillance, response protocols

Care Planning

Each patient requires a comprehensive plan of care developed by the interdisciplinary team, addressing:

  • Medical management and symptom control
  • Nursing care needs
  • Personal care requirements
  • Psychosocial support
  • Spiritual care
  • Volunteer services
  • Bereavement support for family
  • Medication and equipment needs

Plans must be reviewed and updated at least every 15 days and whenever patient condition changes.

Documentation Standards

Maintain thorough clinical documentation including:

  • Assessment and reassessment records
  • Visit notes for all disciplines
  • Medication records
  • Interdisciplinary team meeting notes
  • Family communication logs
  • Advance directive documentation

8. Marketing and Community Outreach

Building referral relationships is essential for hospice census development.

Referral Relationship Development

Physicians and Medical Practices – Primary care physicians, oncologists, cardiologists, and nephrologists manage patients who may benefit from hospice. Education and relationship building are essential.

Hospital Discharge Planners – Case managers and social workers identify hospitalized patients appropriate for hospice referral.

Skilled Nursing Facilities – Residents with terminal conditions may elect hospice services while remaining in the facility.

Cancer Centers and Oncology Practices – Oncologists often introduce hospice discussions with patients.

Community Organizations – Faith communities, senior centers, and advocacy organizations connect with families seeking end-of-life resources.

Strong connections with hospital discharge planners, oncology centers, primary care networks, and community organizations drive consistent referrals and census growth.

Education and Awareness

Provider Education – Offer continuing education programs on end-of-life care, advance care planning, and hospice benefits.

Community Presentations – Present at community groups, faith organizations, and senior services about hospice care and advance directives.

Website and Digital Presence – Create professional website with clear information about services, staff, and how to access care.

Reputation Building

Hospice referrals depend heavily on reputation. Focus on:

  • Outstanding clinical care and family support
  • Responsive communication with referral sources
  • Community involvement and visibility
  • Measuring and sharing quality outcomes

9. Maintain Compliance and Prepare for Inspections

Ongoing compliance protects patients, your license, and your certification.

Continuous Compliance

Documentation Quality – Ensure complete, accurate, contemporaneous clinical documentation supporting care provided.

Staff Credentials – Maintain current licensure, certifications, and training for all clinical staff.

Quality Monitoring – Track quality indicators, patient/family satisfaction, and outcomes.

Policy Updates – Keep policies current with regulatory changes and best practices.

Survey Readiness

CDPHE conducts periodic surveys for state licensure. Medicare-certified programs also undergo certification surveys. Prepare by:

  • Maintaining organized, accessible records
  • Ensuring staff understand survey process and can articulate policies
  • Keeping facility/operations in continuous compliance condition
  • Conducting mock surveys to identify gaps
  • Addressing previous deficiencies completely

When deficiencies are cited, respond promptly with detailed plans of correction and implement changes immediately.

Complaint Response

Have procedures for investigating and responding to patient/family complaints. Document all complaints and resolutions, and use feedback to improve care.

10. Frequently Asked Questions

How long does it take to become licensed and Medicare-certified?

State licensing typically takes 3-4 months from complete application. Medicare certification adds another 3-6 months. Total timeline from startup to full operations is typically 6-12 months.

What are the startup costs for a hospice program?

Home-based hospice programs typically require $250,000-$500,000 for licensing, initial staffing, equipment, and operating reserves. Inpatient facilities require significantly more capital.

What qualifications does a hospice medical director need?

The medical director must be a licensed physician (MD or DO) with knowledge of palliative care and terminal illness management. Hospice and Palliative Medicine board certification is preferred but not required.

How many patients does a new hospice typically serve?

New programs often start with 20-50 patients simultaneously, growing as referrals increase. Break-even typically requires consistent census of 35-50+ patients depending on operational structure.

Can hospice patients receive curative treatment?

By electing hospice, patients agree to forgo curative treatment for their terminal diagnosis. They may still receive treatment for conditions unrelated to the terminal diagnosis.

Conclusion

Starting a hospice program in Colorado offers a meaningful opportunity to serve patients and families during life’s most difficult transitions. The combination of an aging population, geographic service gaps in rural areas, and growing acceptance of hospice care creates favorable conditions for well-prepared providers.

Success requires thorough understanding of CDPHE and Medicare regulations, commitment to interdisciplinary care excellence, and strong referral relationships. By following this comprehensive guide—from initial planning through ongoing compliance—you can navigate the licensing process efficiently and build a program that honors patients’ end-of-life wishes.
